Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets of feature types and score bins. For each group $t\in\{1,2\}$, let $N_t>0$ be its total mass and let $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$ satisfy $\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}=1$. Let $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ be the probability of the positive binary outcome $Y=1$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A randomized risk assignment consists of scores $v_b\in[0,1]$ for $b\in\mathcal B$ and a single matrix $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$ with $\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}X_{\sigma b}=1$ for each $\sigma$; conditional on feature type $\sigma$, the assignment chooses bin $b$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}$, independently of group and outcome. Thus, for a group-$t$ individual chosen according to its feature distribution, $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$, and the assigned score is $S=v_B$. The expected positive mass is $\mu_t=N_t\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$, and the group base rate is $\rho_t=\mu_t/N_t$.

The assignment is **calibrated within group $t$** if for every $b\in\mathcal B$,
$$
\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}=v_b\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}a_{t\sigma}X_{\sigma b}.
$$
This cross-multiplied condition also covers bins with zero assigned mass. The instance permits perfect prediction when $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$ for every feature type with $a_{1\sigma}+a_{2\sigma}>0$; a score assignment is perfectly predictive when $S=Y$ almost surely in each group.

derivations.claim: For each $j$, the threshold indicator is $\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$. Hence $\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^+\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$. Integrating this finite sum term by term gives $\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^+s_j=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]$.
The same indicator calculation gives $\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^-\mathbf1_{[0,s_j]}(u)$ and $\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du=\sum_{j=1}^m w_j^-s_j=\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]$.

Let $\Sigma$ and $\mathcal B$ be nonempty finite sets, and let $t\in\{1,2\}$ index two groups. In group $t$, feature type $\sigma$ has proportion $a_{t\sigma}\ge0$, where $\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}=1$, and total mass $N_t>0$. The positive binary outcome $Y=1$ has probability $p_\sigma\in[0,1]$ for feature type $\sigma$, with the same $p_\sigma$ in both groups. A common randomized assignment sends feature type $\sigma$ to bin $b\in\mathcal B$ with probability $X_{\sigma b}\ge0$, where $\sum_bX_{\sigma b}=1$, independently of group and outcome; bin $b$ has score $v_b\in[0,1]$. Set $\rho_t=\sum_\sigma a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma$ and $\mu_t=N_t\rho_t$. Assume $0<\mu_t<N_t$ for each group, so both outcome classes have positive mass. Define the mean score among positive outcomes and among negative outcomes in group $t$ by
$$
\alpha_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}v_b}{\rho_t},\qquad \beta_t=\frac{\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma}\sum_{b\in\mathcal B}a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}v_b}{1-\rho_t},
$$
where the finite group law is $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=1,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}p_\sigma X_{\sigma b}$ and $\Pr_t(\Sigma=\sigma,Y=0,B=b)=a_{t\sigma}(1-p_\sigma)X_{\sigma b}$. The assignment is **balanced for positive outcomes** if $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, and **balanced for negative outcomes** if $\beta_1=\beta_2$. Fix a group $t\in\{1,2\}$ with a finite joint law $\Pr_t$ for a binary outcome $Y\in\{0,1\}$ and a score $S$ taking finitely many values in $[0,1]$, and assume $\Pr_t(Y=1)>0$ and $\Pr_t(Y=0)>0$. For each threshold $u\in[0,1]$, define the true-positive rate $\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=1)$ and the false-positive rate $\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)=\Pr_t(S\ge u\mid Y=0)$. These are finite step functions and
$$
\mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=1]=\int_0^1\operatorname{TPR}_t(u)\,du,\qquad \mathbb E_t[S\mid Y=0]=\int_0^1\operatorname{FPR}_t(u)\,du.
$$
The integrals are ordinary Riemann integrals of the finite step functions.

derivations.claim: Set $\alpha=\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and $\beta=\beta_1=\beta_2$ by [F3]; since $S\in[0,1]$, both common means lie in $[0,1]$. By [F4], these means are the respective areas under the groups' true-positive-rate and false-positive-rate threshold functions. Summing the calibration identity [F2] over all bins gives $\mathbb E_t[S]=\Pr_t(Y=1)=\rho_t$ for each $t$. Partitioning this finite expectation by $Y$ gives $\rho_t=\rho_t\alpha+(1-\rho_t)\beta$, hence $\rho_t(1-\alpha)=(1-\rho_t)\beta$.

If $\alpha<1$, then $1-\alpha>0$ and $1-\rho_t>0$, so the last identity yields $\rho_t/(1-\rho_t)=\beta/(1-\alpha)$ for both groups. Therefore $\rho_1/(1-\rho_1)=\rho_2/(1-\rho_2)$; cross-multiplication gives $\rho_1=\rho_2$. If instead $\alpha=1$, the identity and $1-\rho_t>0$ give $\beta=0$.

In the branch $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=0$, each group has positive and negative mass by hypothesis. The score has finite support in $[0,1]$, so a conditional mean of one on $Y=1$ is possible only when every positive-mass score value is $1$; a conditional mean of zero on $Y=0$ is possible only when every positive-mass score value is $0$. Thus $S=Y$ almost surely in both groups. If a feature type $\sigma$ with positive mass had $0<p_\sigma<1$, both outcomes would have positive mass at $\sigma$. The same assignment row $X_{\sigma b}$ is used for both outcomes [F1], so their conditional score laws would agree, contradicting concentration at scores $1$ and $0$, respectively. Hence every occupied feature type has $p_\sigma\in\{0,1\}$, which permits perfect prediction.
